Hughes, students have been successful in presenting at conferences, publishing research, and securing coveted graduate school offers and professional positions.
GWS upholds Goal 4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice-Strategy 2 and 3 GWS' mission as a discipline is to center human rights, equality, dignity, anti-racism, and social justice in all we do.
GWS does this especially well through its transformative and topical curriculum by offering courses that include Black Feminisms, Black Masculinities, Latinx Masculinities, Transgender Lives and Cultures, and other courses in the field of Queer Studies.
Central to this mission, is a yearly program of events that prioritizes diversity, inclusion, and social justice.
GWS actively recruits a variety of students and is one of the most diverse discipline on campus.
We have the highest number of students of color and other minoritized groups among our majors and minors.
Through our scholarship funding, GWS prioritizes need-based decisions and the fair distribution of resources across eligible students.
GWS also has a single-mother Carlson scholarship that offers the student full-tuition for the duration of their matriculation.

As a Department, GWS is poised to extend anti-racist principles and actions at URI, the RI community, and beyond.
GWS embodies key URI Strategic Goals, in particular in the area of Embrace Diversity and Social Justice.
The designation of GWS as a Department goes hand in hand with the demand for an Africana Studies Department.
GWS joins African Studies in upholding the core values of diversity, inclusion, antiracism, and social justice in all areas of academic life at URI.

6 We join AAF and other departments in advancing a more diverse, inclusive, and anti-racist university that will better serve our community of students, faculty, administrators, and staff. 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
GWS becoming a department does not impact other departments and programs.
As discussed above, GWS has operated as a department for many years without impacting other academic units.
Rather, GWS has collaborated closely with other academic units to uphold its interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary discipline.
With department designation, GWS will fortify and broaden collaboration across the disciplines.
D.
INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.

Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g., loss of students or revenues), provide a specific rationale of the assumptions make in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
URI will lead the way in RI by creating a Department of Gender and Women's Studies.
Regionally, there are several departments that include UMass-Dartmouth, Connecticut College, Wellesley College, and Simmons College.
None of our similar peer institutions has departments in Women's Studies (JMU, UNH, UVM, etc.).
Of our "aspire to be like" peer institutions, the University of Delaware and University of Virginia have departments in Women's Studies, UCONN does not.
This moment offers an ideal opportunity for URI to take a leadership position by designating GWS as a department and rise to the level of two out of three "aspiring to be like" institutions.

There will be no impacts to other RI institutions in terms of loss of students or revenue.
Nearly 99% of our majors come from within URI and select GWS as a second major in their sophomore year or as a first semester junior.
All major RI public and private institutions offer Women's Studies or similar programs like Gender and Sexuality Studies.
These institutions have successfully recruited students for their programs over the years.
There is no reason to believe that a change in GWS designation as a department will change that pattern. 2.

The goal will be to enhance future research and programmatic collaborations and student learning opportunities. 3.

GWS does not require new facilities and capital equipment for this change.

GWS has been housed in Roosevelt Hall since its establishment as a program in 1978.
GWS will remain at its current location on the third floor of Roosevelt Hall and occupy the same offices of 317, 315, 313, 311, 316 and 314.
We have a seminar room, 311, that we use for multiple purposed such as small classes, faculty and student meetings, workshops, candidate interviews, and social events.
GWS courses are scheduled across the university via general scheduling and we use Roosevelt 311 for our smaller classes.
All spaces are in compliance with ADA requirements. 2.

GWS does not require new resources for this structural change.
GWS already functions as a department with its own budget, chartfield strings, URI Foundation accounts, student scholarships, and research funds.
Central Data for Fall 2019 show that GWS delivers many credit hours, 2,010 per 6.8 FTE for a 297.8 ratio.
When compared to the overall URI's Central Data from F2018, GWS has been delivering a lot of value on minimal resources for many years now. 2.

No extra resources are required for the organizational change.

Administrative staff also provides programming and social event support.
GWS runs from 3-4 events every semester that include the Dana Shugar, Carlson, and other colloquia.

The establishment of the Queer Studies minor (to be initiated in Fall 21) and other curricular innovations in the areas of black feminisms and masculinities studies will increase student interest in GWS. FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday October 7, 2026 - Time: 10:00 am to 12:00 Pastore Hall Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items: Staff will work with Pres.
Preisser on the script and slides for next week’s meeting.
Pres.
Preisser will finalize the “Liaisons” draft and create accompanying slides.
Staff will update the FSEC’s project tracker based on recent progress and pending senate action.
Staff will finalize the list of joint committee assignments so it can be attached to the FS meeting agenda and, regarding the JCODL in particular, will make sure relevant committee staff are notified of new members. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 10:03 am.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, and Chen were present.
Past President Travis Williams was also on hand. 2.
Minutes for approval 2.1 Minutes of the 09/30/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited by the Committee. 2.2 Minutes of the 9/17/26 FS meeting - The minutes were approved for posting as edited by the Committee.
They will be docketed for action at the 10/15/26 Faculty Senate meeting. 3.

Priority Items and New Business (50 minutes) 3.1.
Meeting Prep - 10/15/26 Faculty Senate Meeting - see also microphone duties - FSEC worked through the draft agenda item by item and approved the agenda for posting.
Items discussed included following, along with: The student-led Land Acknowledgment presentations will not be shared in advance but will be archived.
Any fliers brought by the presenters for related events will be made available near the sign-in area at the meetings.
A reminder about the Brightspace purge will be added to the announcements. 3.1.1 Status of Legislation: ● Course withdrawals legislation - will be tabled to November to give the proposer time to meet with TAAC and consider/incorporate other feedback. ● Special/Standing Committees - Draft language was updated and the accompanying slides were reviewed in detail.
The item should be ready for action: CBUN should have time to review the edits before the meeting. 3.1.2 Selection of Nominating Committee - Three nominees have agreed to serve and FSEC agreed to advance the slate of members.

Nominations will be invited from the floor but with a disclaimer about putting nominees ‘on the spot’ without them having time to consider workload and other factors. 3.1.1 Forum - College Liaisons- FSEC members offered edits to the draft legislation.
Pres.
Preisser will finalize the slides before next Thursday.
A significant subject of debate was the timing of liaison selection since serving in this capacity will be an additional duty and potential liaisons may want to know their other committee duties before committing to the role.
FSEC members questioned whether standing committee chairs should be automatically precluded from serving as liaisons.
Feedback from the forum may help clarify answers to these questions.
Pres.
Preisser hopes to reserve 20 minutes for the forum (5 for presentation and 15 for feedback). 1

3.2.
Current Project Tracker and Advance Agenda Setting updates - FSEC is on target with the priorities outlined in the tracker over the summer.
After next week’s senate meeting, the active steps and completion columns will need to be updated. 3.3.
Committee Assignment Updates 3.6.1 Standing Committee Members - updates The standing committees are set except that the College of Business will need to replace a senator who resigned. 3.6.2 Joint Committees - Still a work in progress - staff has had a lot of back and forth with various nominees and it is still hoped that all assignments can be finalized on 10/15.
Needing particular attention is the JCODL, whose membership was the subject of recent legislation. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.
Graduate student-related concerns - Sen.
Daniels followed up, noting he had a productive exchange with the Graduate School Dean, who suggested a procedural fix could solve the ‘enrollment holds’ problem his students have been having without making changes to the University Manual.

In short, providing a timeline to completion for those part time students who are progressing through their programs outside the normal timeframes, would allow the Dean to proactively notify Enrollment Services so that holds are not placed.
It was suggested that this process be piloted by Sen.
Daniels’ computer science students and if the process works, it could be expanded to others.
Sen.
Trimm noted that the English Department has similarly affected students so this might be a good option for them as well.
Sens.
Trimm and Daniels are encouraged to work with their departments and the graduate school to try out the recommended procedural ‘fix.’ The matter can be brought back to FSEC’s attention when and/or if necessary. 4.2.
Curricular Practical Training (CPT) (Internship concerns follow-up from Sen.
Daniels) There had been concern that the ICE guidance memo on CPT might be interpreted and enforced in the most draconian way, and FSEC agreed in their last meeting that Sen.
Daniels would request guidance from Vice Provost for Global Initiatives Johnson.
VP Johnson noted there is a current lawsuit about this issue and she discouraged any action while the challenge plays out.

There are concerns about students in the meantime, however, as summer 2027 internship applications are often due by December.
This timeline makes it very difficult to advise and assist students in a meaningful way as they consider their training options.
FSEC agreed to table this discussion until a legal update is available from either the Vice Provost’s or the General Counsel’s office. 4.3.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - No new concerns were submitted but FSEC circled back to a couple of past concerns.
Future FS agendas will include brief updates to close the loop on anonymous inquiries.
Regarding a concern about a conflict of interest in A&S, FS President Preisser noted he had communicated with the dean who is aware of the perceived conflict. 4.4.
Continued Discussion - Creation of College Liaisons - Pres.
Preisser shared a draft of the proposed language which will be shared at the 10/15 Forum.
Several suggestions were offered and additional faculty feedback will be solicited during the Forum. 4.5.
Ongoing Discussion - Creation of a Programs Subcommittee (current draft); future forum - Draft proposal language will be shared with both the CBUM and CASC, who are 2

expected to return comments. FSEC members are encouraged to comment as well. There will be time to incorporate feedback before the December Forum. 5. Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1. Updates 5.1.1 Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others ● APC meeting of 10/13/26 - Pres. Preisser will confirm with the BAC Chair that the committee is receiving draft policies that may be of interest to faculty. i. Other Updates - Budget; College level governance concerns, etc. FSEC briefly moved into Executive Session to wrap up discussion of a college level governance issue related to Senate oversight over curricular matters . Returning to regular session, there was a brief discussion of the announcement that the current Provost intends to leave that role next year. It is not yet known what the job description/job ad for a new Provost will look like or how that search will be run. Questions pertained to whether or not the anticipated medical school will have its own Provost, a dean under the Provost’s position as currently understood, or some other structure altogether. It is not clear when those details will be forthcoming. 6. New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. None. 7. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. Pres. Preisser noted that Saturday’s apple picking event went very well and the FSEC considered making this an annual event for the faculty senate. Pres. Preisser also noted that he has secured a student worker to help the Retired Faculty Association (RFA) create a website that can be linked or otherwise integrated with the faculty senate’s pages. 8. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 11:35 am. 3

Article III, Section 7 – Ethical conduct. The people of the State of Rhode Island believe that public officials and employees must adhere to the highest standards of ethical conduct, respect the public trust and the rights of all persons, be open, accountable and responsive, avoid the appearance of impropriety and not use their position for private gain or advantage.
WHAT IS “ETHICAL” CONDUCT?

Ethics: a standard or philosophy of right and wrong human behavior based on logical reasoning So… “Ethical Conduct” is the type of behavior that a logical person would agree is the “right” thing to do under the circumstances But - People have different ideas about what makes behavior “right” or “wrong”
Ethics based on CULTURE – Many people think that whether something is “ethical” depends on the setting in which it occurs, taking into account the local culture, habits and customs.

Ethics based on CONSEQUENCES - Ethical or unethical conduct is determined by examining the results. Ethical conduct is behavior that results in more positive results than negative results, in quantity and quality.

Ethics based on CHARACTER - Ethical conduct is determined by asking, “What would a virtuous person do under the circumstances?” The focus is on one’s character and motives. I am an honest, upstanding person, so how could I violate the Code of Ethics?

Focus on your ACTION, not the result ! ! ! The Code of Ethics tells us what actions to avoid, without regard to culture, consequence, or character. Ethical or unethical conduct is determined NOT by looking at the results, but at the conduct itself and judging its inherent rightness or wrongness.
Who is subject to the Code of Ethics? All elected and appointed officials and employees of state and local government, boards, commissions and agencies shall be subject to the Code of Ethics.

A person subject to the Code of Ethics . . . may not participate in any matter in which he or she has an interest, financial or otherwise, which is in substantial conflict with the proper discharge of his or her duties in the public interest. A substantial conflict of interest occurs if it is reasonably foreseeable that he or she or any family member or business associate, or any business by which he or she is employed or represents, will derive a direct monetary gain or suffer a direct monetary loss by reason of his or her official activity.

Reasonably foreseeable The conflict need not be certain to occur, but the probability must be greater than “conceivably.” Business Associates Your “business associates” are any persons or entities that you are joined with to achieve a common financial objective. These include not only your business partners, but also people you have hired such as an attorney, accountant, realtor, contractor, etc. These also include any businesses or organizations, even if not-for-profit, for which you are an officer or serve on the Board of Directors.
Ongoing Business Association parties conducting ongoing business transactions outstanding accounts anticipated future relationship
Who are my family members? Whether by blood, marriage, or adoption: Spouse Grandchildren Parents Aunts/Uncles Children Nieces/Nephews Siblings First Cousins Grandparents

A conflict of interest is a situation where a person’s public duties impact, or involve, his or her private life. ► It is not unethical to have a conflict of interest. ► It does not violate the Code of Ethics to have a conflict of interest. ► It is not the conflict that is the problem; rather, the potential problem is in a failure to identify and manage the conflict.

Do I have a conflict of interest? Ask yourself . . . Is it “reasonably foreseeable” that: A decision I am helping to make as part of my public duties, will result in a financial benefit or detriment to: Me; or My family or household member; or My outside employer; or My business associate?

Ask yourself: Even if there is no financial impact, is a family member, household member, employer or business associate a party to, or participating in, the matter being discussed? If the answer is “Yes,” then you have a conflict of interest and you must recuse from any participation in the matter.

HOW TO RECUSE 1. Complete a Statement of Conflict of Interest form. 2. Present the original to your presiding officer, appointing authority, director, or immediate supervisor. 3. Send a copy to the Ethics Commission.

Nepotism - You may not participate in any matter as part of your public duties if there is reason to believe or expect that any person within your family or a household member . . . • is a party to or participant in such matter; or • will derive a direct monetary gain; or • will suffer a direct monetary loss; or • obtain an employment advantage.

These prohibitions apply regardless of whether a family or household member is objectively the most qualified candidate for a job, or is deserving of promotion. The policy underlying the prohibitions against nepotism in the Code recognizes that it is difficult for any person to be truly objective when considering matters impacting family/household members and, additionally, furthers the constitutionally founded goal of avoiding the appearance of impropriety.

► Recusal is not the same as abstaining, which may mean that the public official will not vote, but has participated in discussions on a matter. ► Recusal means that you are not participating in deliberations or debates, making recommendations, giving advice, considering findings, or in any other way assuming responsibility for or participating in any aspect of the work or decision-making relating to the matter where there are potential conflicts of interest.

Recusal does not mean that the public official must leave the room if it is an open meeting, although it is best practice to do so. However, if the public body is in executive session, once the official has recused, he or she has no more right to be in the room than any other member of the general public.

Secondary Employment You may have a private or public sector job in addition to your state/municipal position; however, you may not accept outside employment that impairs your independence of judgment or that induces you to disclose confidential government information.

When considering potential conflicts of interest regarding secondary employment, the Commission examines a number of factors: • nexus between public duties & private employment • whether such work is completed outside normal work hours & without use of public resources • whether the official/employee would appear before own agency • whether such work would be conducted outside of areas over which official/employee has decision-making jurisdiction • whether official/employee would use his or her public position to solicit business or customers

The Appearance of Impropriety The appearance of impropriety is a phrase referring to a situation which to a layperson without knowledge of the specific circumstances might seem to raise ethics questions.

The Appearance of Impropriety When enacting the Code of Ethics, the General Assembly included as one of its legislative purposes the elimination of impropriety. The legislature did not, however, make the appearance of impropriety a violation of the law.

WHAT IS AN ADVISORY OPINION? An advisory opinion is a legal interpretation of the Rhode Island Code of Ethics issued by the Ethics Commission which provides specific guidance about a particular and impending circumstance. Advisory opinions are based upon the representations made by, or on behalf of, the persons or entities requesting them, and are not the result of adversarial or investigative proceedings.

WHO CAN REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? A person subject to the Code of Ethics may request an advisory opinion about a particular provision of the Code which may affect him or her. WHEN SHOULD I REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? If you believe you may face a real or potential conflict of interest, the time to request an advisory opinion is before you take any official action.

HOW DO I REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? To request an advisory opinion, you must either mail or hand-deliver to the Commission a letter containing your original signature and the following information: • Your name, official position, and a description of your duties; • Your daytime telephone number and e-mail address; • Briefly, the name, jurisdiction and powers of your agency, commission, or office; • The nature of the potential conflict; • A summary of relevant facts; and • Any time constraints.
